Invariant-Driven Classification: introduce and employ invariants (depth proﬁle, δ(G), trace fields, quaternion algebras) to distinguish objects up to commensurability or isomorphism.

Summary Description: Max Forester is a prominent mathematician at the University of Oklahoma whose research bridges geometric group theory, low-dimensional topology, and spectral theory. His work extensively develops and applies Bass–Serre theory and deformation-space techniques to understand group actions on trees, proving accessibility-type finiteness results for finite-index splittings via collapse/fold methods and δ(G)–based bounds. He has advanced the theory of Generalized Baumslag–Solitar groups, constructing and analyzing lattices in Aut(Xm,n) and introducing depth proﬁles as robust commensurability invariants, revealing intricate lattice behaviors and nontrivial phenomena such as incommensurability with isomorphic Cayley graphs. In hyperbolic 3-manifold topology, Forester collaborates on minimal-complexity manifolds, providing explicit combinatorial models (ideal triangulations, spines, ℓ-chains) and leveraging Kojima decomposition, Dehn fillings, and arithmetic invariants to classify and compute volumes and symmetry structures. He also co-authors influential work on the topology of reflectionless canonical systems, describing PSL(2,R)–orbit decompositions across Dirac/Schrödinger/Jacobi regimes via Krein theory and Herglotz representations, illustrating the breadth of his mathematical toolkit. In the realm of scl, Forester develops a linear-programming framework based on taut surfaces and turn-path encodings to prove rationality and computability results for stable commutator length in non-filling curves on surfaces. Across these domains, his research is characterized by a unifying emphasis on canonical models, computable invariants, and the interaction of combinatorial, geometric, and analytic methods to achieve precise classifications, bounds, and constructions.
